first_design.rule: One property, from which every case follows: memory that a memory manager's instance gave out is reached only while the instance still holds it for that use. A value "reaches" an instance in two cases: it holds an address in memory the instance gave, or it will call the instance later. That covers a value made in the instance, an owner of it, a weakref link to it (the link keeps the block through the weak count in the block's header), a view into such memory, and anything that holds or captures one of these: a struct, a list, an iterator, a function value's state, an error, a token. Four consequences follow. (1) Bound: a value that reaches an instance lives no longer than the instance. Keeping it longer is E3063, and handing it to C, which keeps it, is such a keeping. (2) Exact ends: such a value is ended by exactly the operation that gives back the memory it reaches, and by nothing else. The instance's end and reset() give back everything. A scope's end gives back only what that scope gave. Allocating and opening a scope give back nothing. (3) Thread: a value's growth and its end call its instance, so the value holds a link to the instance. The link is never written, and it is stored only where verdict 47/107 keep the word. It is a changing link (sharedref mut, one thread, verdict 164) when the manager's allocate/deallocate/reallocate change their object, as an Arena's move its cursor. It is a read-only link (ref) when the manager changes its state only through Atomic or a lock, or has no state. So where the value may go, a thread_shared value included, follows from P01's own rule: markers come from contents, and verdict 165 checks at the making line. (4) Which types: `using A` follows every type whose declaration leaves a manager to its maker. That is a holder that may give a block back (owns, shares, shares mut, thread_shared, weakref), a class, and any type that says it takes one (`struct SlotMap using A:`). The library's String and collections say it the same way, so a program's own container takes `using` as theirs do. The kind of manager is named only where a value may be grown, replaced or ended; a name that can do neither (a plain parameter, a view) accepts a value from any manager.
first_design.spec_text:
NEW [ALC-6] **Memory a manager gave is reached only while the manager holds it.** A value *reaches* an instance of a memory manager when it holds an address in memory the instance gave out, or will call the instance: a value made in it ([ALC-1]); an owner of such a value; a `weakref` link to one, which keeps its block through the weak count ([OBJ-3]); a view into such memory ([ARN-1], [LT-1]); and every value that holds or captures one of these (a struct, a list, an iterator, a function value's state, an error, a token). A value that only names a position (a `Handle`, an index) reaches nothing. Every value that reaches an instance:
1. lives no longer than the instance. Keeping or returning it where it would outlive the instance is `E3063` ([LT-4], [LT-45]). A hand-over to C that keeps it ([FFI-54], [OWN-12]) is such a keeping: "C keeps `w` after `level` ends; make it without `using level`". A value put in through a `ref mut` parameter reaches what it reached in the callee ([LT-47]).
2. is ended by exactly the operation that gives back the memory it reaches, and by no other. The instance's end and `reset()` give back all of the instance's memory. The end of a scope ([ARN-6]) gives back what that scope gave. Allocating, and opening a scope, give back nothing. A use after the memory it reaches was given back is `E3060`. Giving that memory back while such a value is still used is `E3021` ([ALC-5]).
3. holds a link to the instance. The link is written nowhere and is stored only where [ALC-1] keeps the word. It is a changing link, a kept `sharedref mut` ([LT-46]), when the manager's `allocate`, `deallocate` or `reallocate` change their object (worked out from their bodies, [EXC-15]), as an `Arena`'s move its cursor. Otherwise it is a kept `ref`: the manager changes its state only through `Atomic` or a lock (verdict 3), or has none. So a value made in an instance its methods change stays on one thread (verdict 164; `E7015`, `E7008`). Scoped tasks use it where it is, and its growth and end count as changes of the instance ([THR-11], [EFF-24]; two tasks: `E7007`). A value made in an instance that its methods only read is `Send` and `ThreadShared` exactly as a `ref` of the manager is ([THR-8], [THR-9]). A manager with one instance holds no link, and its methods are checked as any call wherever a value's growth or end may run them ([THR-20]).

CHANGED [TYP-46] / [ALC-1] (the closed list goes). `using A` follows every type whose declaration leaves a manager to its maker:
* a holder that may give a block back (`owns`, `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared` or `weakref` before a type: `target: weakref Enemy using LevelArena`);
* a class type;
* a type that says it takes one, with `using` after its name in its declaration (`[T]` above `struct SlotMap using A:`; `class Level using A:`). In its body `A` names the manager kind, and a field typed `using A` takes its memory from the instance the value is made in. The standard library's `String`, `Array`, `Map`, `Set`, `Deque`, `SmallArray`, `BitSet`, `RingBuffer` and `Pool` are declared this way.

`enemies: SlotMap[Enemy] using LevelArena`, made `SlotMap[Enemy]() using current`, makes in `current` its field defaults and what its methods make for those fields without naming an instance. A type takes at most one manager. After any other type, `using` is `E2114`. The message for a struct whose fields have memory but which takes no manager: "`Level` does not say it takes a memory manager, and its fields say where their memory comes from; to give it one, write `struct Level using A:` and `using A` after the fields that take it, or remove `using`". The message for a view: "a view gives nothing back to a manager; remove `using`". A manager written in brackets (`SlotMap[Enemy, LevelArena]`) is `E1010`, whose help gives `SlotMap[Enemy] using LevelArena`, as for `Array[T, A]`. The kind must match only where a value may be grown, replaced or ended: a field, a local, an `owns` or `ref mut` parameter, a `weakref` place (`E2020` otherwise). A plain parameter or a view accepts a value from any manager. `thread_shared T using A` is allowed exactly where the value's end may run on any thread under [ALC-6] 3: an instance its methods only read that is `ThreadShared`, or a manager with one instance whose methods reach no one-thread state. Anything else is `E7015` at the making line ([THR-1], verdict 165).

answers.answer: Decided with no exception for thread_shared. A thread_shared value may end on any thread, and its end gives its block back to its instance, so the instance must be one every thread may give memory back to ([ALC-6] 3). An Arena's allocate moves its cursor, so its link is a changing link that stays on one thread (verdict 164). That makes `thread_shared ... using level` E7015 at the making line, by verdict 165's check. A manager with one instance and no one-thread state (System, Global), or a several-instance manager whose state sits behind a lock or Atomic, is allowed. Such a value is made handed over (RC-4 point 4): every owner is counted in the away count, so no making thread is read and fix 1's 'never from the value' holds.
answers.code:
from std.sync import Atomic
import std.thread

class Stats:
    hits: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)

fn main():
    stats = thread_shared Stats() using System    # a manager every thread may give memory back to
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn() owns stats: stats.hits.fetch_add(1))
    println("done")
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints done. Every owner of `stats` is counted with one atomic add, as Rust's Arc counts. The example's `thread_shared Stats() using level` is E7015 at that line: "`stats` is shared between threads, so its last owner may end on any of them and give its block back to `level` there; `level` is an `Arena`, whose `allocate` moves its cursor, so only this thread may use it; make `stats` without `using level`". A program's own pool whose free list sits in a `Mutex` (`static SLAB: Slab`, then `thread_shared Session() using SLAB`) compiles the same way.

answers.answer: Decided: a scope's end gives back only what the scope gave, so it ends only views into that memory ([ALC-6] 2). Opening a scope gives back nothing. The root, taken from the arena before the scope, stays valid inside the scope and after it. Allocating from the parent while the scope lives stays E3096.

@derive(Zeroable)
struct Tok:
    kind: int

struct Node:
    kind: int

fn parse(ref mut frame: Arena) -> int:
    root = ref mut frame.alloc(owns Node(kind=1))   # kept for the whole parse
    with s = frame.scope():                          # scratch memory, given back when the block ends
        toks = ref mut s.alloc_zeroed[Tok](64)
        toks[0].kind = 2
        root.kind += toks[0].kind                    # root is below the scope's memory
    return root.kind

fn main():
    frame = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)
    println(parse(ref mut frame))
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints 3. The scope's end lowers the cursor to where the scope began, and root lies below that. `frame.alloc(...)` inside the `with` block is E3096 (allocate from `s`). `toks` used after the block is E3060.

answers.answer: Decided, as phase 3 restated it. `using` follows every type whose declaration leaves a manager to its maker. The standard library's String, Array, Map, Set, Deque, SmallArray, BitSet, RingBuffer and Pool all say it in their declarations (`struct Deque using A:`), and a program's own container says it the same way. So no path exists that only the library can take. thread_shared is decided by the thread consequence, not left out by type.

[T]
struct SlotMap using A:                         # takes a memory manager, called A in its body
    slots: Array[Option[T]] using A = []        # from the instance the map is made in
    free: Array[int] using A = []

class Enemy:
    hp: int

struct Level:
    names: Array[String] using Arena
    title: String using Arena
    enemies: SlotMap[Enemy] using Arena

fn load(ref mut current: Arena) -> Level:
    return Level(names=[String("orc")] using current, title=String("Cave") using current, enemies=SlotMap[Enemy]() using current)

fn main():

    lvl = load(ref mut level_mem)

The title's text, the names list's buffer and both of the SlotMap's lists come from `level_mem`. `lvl` lives no longer than `level_mem` (E3063 otherwise). `using Arena` after `int`, after a view, or after a struct that does not say `using A` is E2114, whose help gives the declaration line.

answers.answer: Decided: String declares that it takes a manager, as Array does. So `text: String using Arena` is allowed, and its growth goes back to the arena, as ALC-1's own sentence already says.
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints let. A StrView of `t.text` reaches the arena too: it is ended by `arena.reset()` and refused past the arena's end (E3060, E3063).

other_cases.case: A StrView into an arena-made String, used after `arena.reset()`.
other_cases.settled: The view reaches the arena's memory ([ALC-6]), so the reset ends it. The use after the reset is E3060; with the use placed before the reset, the program compiles.

other_cases.case: Two scoped tasks each pushing to its own list, both lists made in one Arena.
other_cases.settled: Growth calls `level.allocate`, which moves the cursor: both tasks change the instance through a changing link. That is E7007 (two tasks change `level`). One task alone pushing, or the pushes done after the join, compiles. Reads of arena lists from many tasks compile, because a read never touches the manager.

other_cases.case: An arena-made widget handed to C through an `owns` contract (`widget_take(owns w)`), or captured by `thread.spawn`.
other_cases.settled: C, or an unscoped thread, keeps it past every local instance. That is E3063 for C and E7015 for the thread (its instance link stays on one thread). The help says to make it without `using`. `w.into_raw()` inside `unsafe:` is the block's vouching: [UNS-4] now says a raw pointer into a manager's memory is not used after that memory is given back.

other_cases.case: A program's struct `Level` with list fields, written `lvl: Level using Arena`, without `struct Level using A:`.
other_cases.settled: E2114: Level's fields already say where their memory comes from (the built-in manager), and a written field means only what it says (verdict 132's lesson). The help gives `struct Level using A:` plus `using A` on the fields.

other_cases.case: A helper `fn total(xs: Array[int]) -> int` called with an arena-made list, and `fn fill(ref mut xs: Array[int])` called with one.
other_cases.settled: `total` compiles for a list from any manager, because a plain parameter can neither grow nor end the list. `fill` may push, so the kind must match: E2020, with help `ref mut xs: Array[int] using Arena`, or a generic `[A: needs Allocator]` with `using A`.

other_cases.case: A class object made in a lock-based pool, with a weakref link on this thread, handed whole to another thread (verdict 114).
other_cases.settled: The pool's methods only read it, and it is ThreadShared, so the object is Send. Verdict 114 moves its contents to a new block taken from the same pool instance. The old block stays here until its last link ends, then goes back to the pool (allowed from this thread).

other_cases.case: Nested scopes: `with a = frame.scope():` then `with b = a.scope():`, with a view from `a` used after `b` ends.
other_cases.settled: b's end gives back only what b gave, so the view from `a` stays valid until a's end. Views from b used after b's end are E3060.

other_cases.case: A Pool's Handle kept after the pool ends.
other_cases.settled: A handle is a number and reaches no memory, so nothing bounds it. Without the pool it cannot be looked up. A `ref T` from `pool.get(h)` is a view into the pool and is bounded by it, as today.

other_cases.case: A closure capturing an arena-made value, stored in a static, or an AnyError holding an error that views arena text, returned with `?` past the arena.
other_cases.settled: Both reach the instance, so both are E3063. The closure's state block and AnyError's box come from the built-in manager; no declaration names a manager for them, so `fn() using A` is E2114. A program that wants type-erased state in an arena writes `owns dyn I using A`.

other_cases.case: A static instance (`static LEVEL: LockedPool`), with values made in it kept in other statics.
other_cases.settled: A static instance outlives everything, so its values may be kept anywhere, unscoped threads included if its link only reads. A reset of it is E3021 while any value that reaches it may still be used, which is never for a value held in a static.

other_cases.case: A FixedArena over a buffer (`Arena.fixed(ref mut buffer)`), with values made in it.
other_cases.settled: The FixedArena holds a kept ref mut view of the buffer ([ARN-4]), so its values reach the buffer through it, and each is bounded by both.

other_cases.case: A shares mut value made in an Arena, with a sharedref mut link to it held elsewhere.
other_cases.settled: Owners hold the block and the link views it, so both reach the arena and both are bounded. The count block is in arena memory, which the arena keeps until its end or reset, and a reset is refused while either lives.

first_design.prior_art: C++ std::pmr: a container holds a memory_resource* (8 bytes). Program types opt in by declaring allocator_type and getting uses-allocator construction, the same idea as `struct SlotMap using A:`. allocate_shared puts the control block, weak count included, in the resource's memory, so a weak_ptr that outlives a released monotonic_buffer_resource is undefined behaviour (exactly J5-02). A string_view into a released resource is also undefined behaviour. Nothing is checked. Rust (allocator_api, still unstable): Box<T, A>, Vec<T, A>, Rc<T, A> and Weak<T, A> take the allocator as a type parameter. With A = &'a Bump the lifetime 'a bounds every holder, the Weak included, which is facet 1. Send follows the allocator: Box<T, &Bump> is Send only if Bump is Sync, and bumpalo's Bump is not, which is facet 3. bumpalo's reset takes &mut self, so no allocation may be live, which is ALC-5. Rust's shortfalls: unstable for years, and the type parameters are written everywhere (Vec<T, &'a Bump>), which is a readability loss Ember avoids with `using` and inferred regions. A Rust scope API that borrows the arena mutably also refuses J5-19's program, which Ember accepts because a view points into memory, not into the cursor. Ada: a storage pool is named per access type (`for Node_Ptr'Storage_Pool use Level_Pool;`), the place naming the kind, as in verdict 24. Accessibility levels bound the access values, partly with run-time checks. Ada 2012 subpools free a subpool at once with Unchecked_Deallocate_Subpool, an erroneous program if references remain. Zig: an Allocator interface passed explicitly and an ArenaAllocator; containers (ArrayListUnmanaged) take the allocator per call; no lifetime or thread checking, so a use after reset is illegal behaviour that is often not detected. Go: GOEXPERIMENT=arenas checked a use after Free at run time by unmapping pages, and the proposal is on hold. Swift and C#: class instances always come from the runtime heap. Swift's withUnsafeTemporaryAllocation and C#'s stackalloc with scoped Span give scratch buffers only. Where they fall short of safe, C-fast and readable: C++ and Zig are fast but unsafe; Go's check costs at run time and was abandoned; Ada checks partly at run time; Swift and C# give no arenas for objects; Rust is safe and fast but unstable and wordy. The rule takes Rust's two facts (the allocator's lifetime and its thread-safety reach every holder), keeps C++'s one-word cost, and the compiler infers both with nothing written.
first_design.cost: Bound and exact ends (facets 1 and 2): zero at run time, because both are compile-time region checks. A scope's end is one pointer store (the cursor lowered), the same as C. Thread (facet 3): zero at run time; the markers are worked out when compiling. `using` on any declared type: one call of the manager's allocate (static dispatch, inlinable), plus the instance word, 8 bytes per value, only where verdict 107 does not remove it. That matches C++ pmr's pointer per container and Rust's &Bump per Vec. Where verdict 107 removes the word it costs nothing extra, and its measurement stands: a million small values took 191 ms and 28.2 MB against C's 191 ms and 28.2 MB. A weakref link to an arena object costs as any link: one plain add and one subtract of the weak count. The block it keeps is reclaimed at the arena's end or reset, as C's arena reclaims everything. A plain parameter that accepts a list from any manager: zero; the compiler makes one copy of the function per layout, or reads the common fields. A thread_shared value made in a manager is the one case that differs. It is made handed over, so each owner +1 or -1 is one atomic read-modify-write, as Rust's Arc and C++'s shared_ptr pay, instead of biased counting's plain add on the making thread. The measured mechanism (measure-0.9.15/brc/REPORT.md, 'own' pattern) shows a thread's own objects at 43.6 ms with one atomic count against 32.3 ms biased, so 1.35x for this case only. Cross-thread patterns cost the same as the atomic column, and a pipeline is 27% faster than biased_pub on one thread. Memory: the same 32-byte header as every thread_shared value, so zero extra; its home and queue fields stay unused. Reading the maker's id from the value instead, J5-05 B's idea, was measured 13% to 44% slower on cross-thread copying, and fix 1 excludes it. C pays nothing for counting because C has no safe sharing. Nothing in this rule adds a check that runs.

# a parser: a tree kept for the whole parse, scratch memory per statement
# today the scope ends every view into `frame`, so the tree's root must be made after the scratch work
fn parse(ref mut frame: Arena) -> int:
    kind = 1                                         # kept in a local instead of the tree
    with s = frame.scope():
        toks = ref mut s.alloc_zeroed[Tok](64)
        toks[0].kind = 2
        kind += toks[0].kind
    root = ref mut frame.alloc(owns Node(kind=kind)) # made after the scope

    text: String                                     # `String using Arena` is E2114 today
readability.ordinary_after:
fn parse(ref mut frame: Arena) -> int:
    root = ref mut frame.alloc(owns Node(kind=1))    # the tree, made first, as the program means
    with s = frame.scope():
        toks = ref mut s.alloc_zeroed[Tok](64)
        toks[0].kind = 2
        root.kind += toks[0].kind
    return root.kind

struct Token:
    kind: int
    text: String using Arena                         # the token's text in the parse's arena
readability.note: The after version is the same length and reads in the order the program means. A program with no arena (a game loop, a server handler using the built-in manager) is identical before and after: no new word, nothing new to write. The rule's cost falls only on the rare program that links into an arena from something that outlives it: the camera's field then names its kind (`weakref Enemy using Arena`), as an owner's field already must. A program's own container writes `using A` once in its declaration, reusing the language's word. Its users write exactly what they write for the library's types (`SlotMap[Enemy] using Arena`).

first_design.compiler_does: 1. It gives each instance a region, and every value made in it that region. It then follows the region, as it follows views today (LT-45), through every holder of an address in the instance's memory: owners, weakref links, views, iterators, captures, errors, tokens, and values put in through ref mut (LT-47). It refuses a keeping past the instance with E3063, and treats a hand-over to C as a keeping. 2. It splits an arena's memory into nested regions, one per open scope, and treats each give-back as ending exactly the regions it frees: reset and the end free all, a scope's end frees its own. An alloc and a scope's opening touch only the cursor, so they end no view (ARN-1 already separates memory from cursor). 3. It infers whether the manager's allocate, deallocate and reallocate change `this` (EXC-15, the inference every method already gets) and makes the hidden instance link a sharedref mut or a ref accordingly. From that link it derives Send and ThreadShared by THR-8/9 and verdict 164, and checks verdict 165 at a thread_shared making line. It counts a value's growth and end as calls of those methods wherever they may run (EFF-24 for scoped tasks, P05's rule for ends the program does not write). 4. For a block a manager gives to a thread_shared value, it emits the handed-over count sequence from the first owner, chosen statically from the place's `using` kind, so no run-time branch and no maker read. 5. For a type declared `using A`, it fills A from the place's `using M`, defaulting to Global. It makes the parts the making line makes (field defaults, and init's making of `using A` fields) in the named instance, and finds `this`'s instance for later parts from the word verdict 47/107 keep. It places the instance word of a block a weakref may keep inside the block, so the last link can give it back. It dispatches deallocate statically by the kind the place names, weakref places included. 6. For a plain parameter given values from several managers, it makes one copy per layout. Nothing is written by the programmer for any of this, except the `using` that names a kind where a value may grow or end.
first_design.misuse: Every mistake is refused when compiling; nothing in safe code reaches freed or reused memory. A weakref, view, owner, iterator, closure or error that reaches an instance and is kept past it: E3063 at the line that keeps it, with the line that makes the arena in the caller. A hand-over to C of an arena-made value: E3063. A reset, or another give-back, while such a value is still used: E3021, with `mem.drop(owns x)` or the reorder. A use after the give-back: E3060, naming the give-back line. A weakref place without the kind for an arena target: E2020, with the field line. `using` after a number, a view, or a struct that does not declare one: E2114, with the declaration line or 'remove using'. An allocator in brackets: E1010, with the `using` spelling. An arena-made value sent to another thread, captured by thread.spawn, put in a channel, or made thread_shared: E7015, naming the arena and why only its thread may use it (its allocate moves its cursor). Two scoped tasks growing or ending values of one Arena: E7007. Allocating from a parent while its scope lives: E3096. What only unsafe code can do stays the vouching code's promise, never undefined behaviour in safe code: into_raw of an arena value used after the reset (UNS-4), and an Allocator implementation that frees memory through a lock under live values (ALC-2's unsafe promise).

Reused, not revisited: 164 (a sharedref mut link never goes to another thread) is the instance link of a manager whose methods change it. 165 (thread_shared refused at the making line when something in it is not ThreadShared) decides J5-05. 114 (a handed-over object moves) takes its new block from the same instance. 3 (Mutex, Atomic and channels need no ref mut) is why a manager changed only through a lock is read, not changed, by its methods. 86 and EXC-15 (what a method changes is inferred) decide the link's kind. 132 (a written declaration means only what it says) is why a struct's unannotated field stays on the built-in manager and the type must say `using A`. options_for_owner.summary: The one rule. Whatever points into or is served by a manager's memory lives no longer than the manager and ends exactly when its memory is given back. Where it may go follows from the hidden link to the manager. `using` follows every type that says it takes a manager, the library's and the program's alike.
options_for_owner.code:
[T]
struct SlotMap using A:
    slots: Array[Option[T]] using A = []

class Enemy:
    hp: int

class Camera:
    target: weakref Enemy using Arena = None

fn load_level(ref mut cam: Camera, ref mut level: Arena):
    boss = Enemy(hp=500) using level
    cam.target = weakref boss
    names = String("Ogre") using level
    enemies = SlotMap[Enemy]() using level
    with s = level.scope():
        tmp = ref mut s.alloc_zeroed[u8](256)    # scratch; `names` stays valid
    println(names)

fn main():
    level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)
    cam = Camera()
    load_level(ref mut cam, ref mut level)
    if cam.target exists as e:
        println(e.hp)
    else:
        println("gone")
    stats = thread_shared Stats() using level    # E7015: an Arena is used by one thread
options_for_owner.outcome: Without the last line it compiles and prints Ogre, then gone. With the arena made inside load_level, `cam.target = weakref boss` is E3063. The last line is E7015 ("its last owner may end on any thread and give its block back to `level` there"); `thread_shared Stats() using System` compiles. A program's own SlotMap, and String, Deque and the rest, take `using` as Array does.

recommendation.reason: A is the only option that is one rule. The same sentence settles weakref links, views, scopes, tokens, C hand-overs, threads and which types may take `using`, for the library's types and the program's alike, with no exception by type. It refuses exactly the programs that would read freed or reused memory or race on a manager, all when compiling, and accepts the correct ones that B and C refuse: a camera following an arena enemy, a tree kept across scratch scopes, an engine's own SlotMap in a level arena, a thread_shared value in a manager every thread may use. Nothing runs for it. The one run-time difference, Arc-style counting for a thread_shared value in a manager, falls only on that rare case and costs what Rust and C++ pay. Ordinary programs are unchanged. It reuses verdicts 164 and 165 and the inference every method already gets, instead of adding a list.

first_design.open_risks: 1. `struct SlotMap using A:` is a new declaration form, though it reuses the word. The owner may prefer an ordinary type parameter `[T, A: needs Allocator = Global]` filled by `using`, which is existing syntax but leaves a second, bracket spelling to refuse. This is a spelling sub-question to show beside A. 2. A thread_shared value in a manager is made handed over and loses biased counting's 25% gain for its own thread's objects. This exact case is not measured; the 1.35x comes from REPORT.md's 'own' pattern, a mechanism measured on runtime blocks. 3. The instance link's kind is inferred from the manager's method bodies, so a library manager's thread-safety follows its bodies, as EXC-15 already makes every pub method's effects do. The owner may judge this against verdict 108's 'a library's promise does not depend on its body'. If so, the alternative is to require that a manager be ThreadShared and change only through lock or Atomic for its values to be Send. 4. Function values' state blocks and AnyError's box take no `using`, because no declaration names a manager for them. A program wanting closure state in an arena writes `owns dyn I using A`. If the owner wants `fn() using A`, that is checklist 12's 'add the syntax' and a further question. 5. C-kept addresses: facet 1 reaches what C keeps only through a holder on Ember's side. P08's token for retained non-callback pointers (J8-12) must be such a holder, or an arena object given to a `retained` parameter is bounded only by FFI-35a. Answer P08 consistently. 6. Weakref places now name their kind (`weakref Enemy using Arena`). One weakref field cannot mix links to heap and arena objects, as one owner field cannot (verdict 24). 7. P01 (markers from contents) and P05 (an end counts as a call where it may run) are assumed: facet 3 is their rule applied to the instance link, so their wording must name 'what a value reaches' to avoid a gap between groups. 8. Verdict 114's new block taken from the same instance can fail for lack of memory at a hand-over, which is a stop ('out of memory', ALC-4). That is the same as any allocation, but it is a new place where a hand-over may stop.

method1_repair.rule: One property, from which every case follows: memory that a manager's instance gave out is reached only while the instance still holds it, and every step that takes memory from a manager or gives it back goes to the manager the memory came from. All of it is decided when compiling. A value *holds into* an instance when it holds an address in memory the instance gave: a value made in it, an owner of one, a weakref link to one (the link keeps the block through its weak count), a view into such memory, and anything that holds or captures one of these. A value *will call* an instance when it holds none of that memory yet, but its growth, replacement or end, or a making for its parts, would call the instance (an empty list made in it). Both are decided for each place at each point, from what the place last got, as a view's life is, and through a call by the callee's summary. Five consequences follow. (1) Bound: such a value lives no longer than the instance (E3063). Handing it to C, which keeps it, counts as a keeping. (2) Exact ends: of the instance's own operations, only one that gives back memory a value holds into ends that value. Its end and reset() give back all of it, a scope's end gives back what that scope gave, and allocating or opening a scope gives back nothing. This is added to the ends every other rule gives. Giving the memory back while the value lives (a view until its last use, an owner or a link until its end) is E3021. A value that only will call the instance survives a reset. (3) New memory: a value takes its memory from the instance its making line names. Else, for a part its type ties to its own manager, it takes it from the instance its whole value is made in. Else it takes it from the built-in manager. So a copy, a sum or a task's accumulator never takes its source's instance unless the line says so, and a read never calls a manager. (4) Threads: only an owner or a ref mut name makes a value call its instance. So the hidden link to the instance counts toward Send and never toward ThreadShared. It stays on one thread (verdict 164) when the manager's allocate, deallocate or reallocate change their object, as an Arena's do. (5) Kinds: the kind is part of a value's type. Every place that keeps a value beyond a call names it, and none means the built-in manager. A function's parameter takes its caller's kind, and the compiler makes a copy of the function for each kind where its body depends on the kind. A block's type index names its kind, so a dyn or virtual call reaches the method compiled for that kind, and a weakref link, which names no kind, gives the block back there. `using` follows every type whose declaration leaves a manager to its maker: a holder that may end a value (owns, shares, shares mut, thread_shared), a class, and a struct, class or enum declared `using A`. The library's String and collections are declared that way.
method1_repair.spec_text:
NEW [ALC-6] **Memory a manager gave is reached only while the manager holds it.** A value *holds into* an instance of a memory manager when it holds an address in memory the instance gave out. That covers a value made in it ([ALC-1]); an owner of such a value; a `weakref` link to one, which keeps its block through the weak count ([OBJ-3]); a view into such memory ([ARN-1], [LT-1]); and every value that holds or captures one of these (a struct, a list, an iterator, a function value's state, an error, a token). A value *will call* an instance when it holds none of the instance's memory, but its growth, replacement or end, or a making for its parts ([ALC-7] 2), would call the instance. Examples are an empty value made in it (`Array.new_in(frame)` and `[] using frame` take no memory until they first grow) and a value of a type made `using` it whose parts hold nothing yet. A value that only names a position (a `Handle`, an index) does neither. What a place holds into or will call is decided at each point, from what the place last got, as a view's life is ([BRW-2]). Where the compiler follows the place (a local, a part of a local or of a parameter, and through a call by the callee's summary, [EFF-24], [LT-47]), it is decided by what the place holds there. Elsewhere (an element reached by position, a part reached through a link or a shared owner, a static) it is decided by what the program may put there. Every value that holds into or will call an instance:
1. lives no longer than the instance. Keeping or returning it where it would outlive the instance is `E3063` ([LT-4], [LT-45]). A hand-over to C that keeps it ([FFI-35a], [OWN-12]) is such a keeping: "C keeps `w` after `level` ends; make it without `using level`".
2. if it holds into the instance's memory, is ended by the instance's operations that give that memory back, and by no other of the instance's operations. The instance's end gives back all of its memory, and so does any change of it that [ALC-5] allows only while no value holds into its memory (an `Arena`'s `reset()`). A scope's end ([ARN-6]) gives back what that scope gave. Allocating and opening a scope give back nothing. This is added to the ends every other rule gives the value ([BCK-4], [BRW-17]): a view of a list's element ends when the list is cleared, whatever manager gave the list. A use after the memory it holds into was given back is `E3060`. Giving that memory back while the value lives is `E3021`; a view lives until its last use, and an owner or a link until its end, which writes the block's counts. A value that only will call the instance is not ended by a reset: it holds none of the memory, and its next growth takes new memory from the instance.
3. calls the instance's methods only through an owner or a `ref mut` name, by the operations that call it: growth, replacement, end, and a making for its parts. A read-only name never makes its value call the instance: a value made from what it reads takes its memory by [ALC-7]. A link or an owner made from it ([WK-11], [RC-1]) is a value of its own, and a scoped task makes one only to a `thread_shared` target ([THR-2], verdict 166). So the instance link of [LT-4] counts toward `Send`, because an owner may be handed over, and never toward `ThreadShared`, because readers never use it. `T using A` is `ThreadShared` exactly when `T` is. It is `Send` when `T` is and the link may go to another thread: the link is a kept `ref` of the instance when `A`'s `allocate`, `deallocate` and `reallocate` change their object only through `Atomic` or a lock, or not at all (worked out from their bodies, [EXC-15]), and the instance is `ThreadShared`. Otherwise the link is a kept `sharedref mut` (an `Arena`'s methods move its cursor), which stays on one thread (verdict 164, `E7015`, `E7008`). Scoped tasks use such a value where it is. Its growth and end there count as changes of the instance ([THR-11], [EFF-24]; two tasks: `E7007`), and a task's reduction into it uses an accumulator of the task's own ([THR-21]). A manager with one instance holds no link. Its methods are checked as any call wherever a value's growth or end may run them ([THR-20]).

NEW [ALC-7] **Where a new value takes its memory.** Every value made takes its memory, and the kind in its type, from the first of these that applies. That covers a literal, a constructor, `copy of x`, and every value made from another: a clone, a `+` that makes a new `String`, `to_string()`, a conversion, `collect()`, a task's accumulator.
1. The instance named after it on its line: `[0.0, 1.0] using current`; `copy of names using level` makes the copy, and every part of it of that kind, in `level` ([GRM-43]).
2. Else, for a part that a type's declaration ties to its own manager (a field, an element type or a payload written `using A` in a type declared `using A`), the instance its whole value is made in. That covers a field's default; a constructor argument (`SlotMap[int](free=[]) using level` makes `free` in `level`); and what `init`, the type's methods (from the word the value keeps, [ALC-1]) and its `clone` make for such a part.
3. Else the built-in manager, or the one instance of the place's kind when the place's type names a manager with one instance.
A value made for a place whose kind may have several instances, which gets no instance by 1 or 2, is `E2020`: "`x` takes its memory from an `Arena`, and nothing names which; say which: `copy of names using level`". So a value made from another never takes its source's instance unless its line names it. `snapshot = copy of names` is an `Array[String]` from the built-in manager, which may outlive `level`, as C++'s `pmr` copy takes the default resource. The compiler gives a derived or library `clone`, and a hand-written one's makings, the instance the copy is made in.

CHANGED [TYP-46] / [ALC-1] (the closed list goes) **The kind of manager is part of a value's type. A place that keeps the value names it, and a parameter takes its caller's.** `using A` follows every type whose declaration leaves a manager to its maker:
* a holder that may end a value: `owns`, `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` before a type (`mesh: owns Mesh using LevelArena`);
* a class type;
* a struct, class or enum that says it takes one, with `using` after its name, or for a class after its base list: `[T]` above `struct SlotMap using A:`; `class Level using A:`; `class Boss(Enemy) using A:`; `enum Expr using A:`. In its body `A` names the manager kind, and a part written `using A` takes its memory from the instance the value is made in ([ALC-7] 2). A derived class takes its base's manager, so `using` on a class whose base takes one is `E2114`. Before such a type, `owns`, `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` with `using A` gives the block and the type's `A` one manager. The standard library's `String`, `Array`, `Map`, `Set`, `Deque`, `SmallArray`, `BitSet`, `RingBuffer` and `Pool` are declared this way.
A type takes at most one manager. After any other type, `using` is `E2114`, with these messages:
* a number;
* a view: "a view gives nothing back to a manager; remove `using`";
* a `weakref` link: "a link takes no memory of its own, and its target's block goes back to the manager it came from; remove `using`";
* a struct that does not say it takes one: "`Level` does not say it takes a memory manager, and its fields say where their memory comes from; to give it one, write `struct Level using A:` and `using A` after the fields that take it, or remove `using`".
A manager written in brackets (`SlotMap[Enemy, LevelArena]`, `Array[T, A]`) is `E1010`, whose help gives the `using` spelling.

Every place that keeps a value beyond a call names its kind, and none means the built-in manager: a field, a static, an element type, a payload, a result, a local whose type is written, and a function type's parameter. A value of another kind given to one is `E2020`: `return [String("orc")] using level` under `-> Array[String]` gets the help `-> Array[String] using Arena`. A local whose type is not written takes its value's kind.

A function's parameter (`this` included) whose type has no `using` takes the kind its caller's value has. The function is compiled once for each kind its callers pass where its body depends on the kind, and once where it does not (verdict 88's copies). The body depends on the kind when it grows, replaces, ends or hands over the value, makes an owner of it, sends it to another thread, or makes values for its `using A` parts. A line of the function that puts the value where another kind is named is `E2020` at the call, naming that line. A call that one body serves for every caller (through a function value, or a `dyn` or `virtual` method) takes the kind each parameter's type says. It accepts any kind where no function that may be reached depends on it ([LT-1]: by the code of each kind that may reach it). `this` of a class object reaches the method compiled for its block's kind ([OBJ-2]). `thread_shared T using A` is allowed exactly where `T using A` is `Send` and `T` is `ThreadShared` ([ALC-6] 3, verdict 165). Otherwise it is `E7015` at the making line.

CHANGED [ALC-1] (the instance word): "A value whose manager may have several instances keeps its instance's address, one word, wherever a later step takes memory from the instance or gives memory back to it. Such steps are its growth, its end, a making for its `using A` parts ([ALC-7] 2), a move to a new block at a hand-over ([THR-2]), and a link's give-back of its block. Verdict 107's two kinds of manager keep the word only where such a step remains. In a manager that frees nothing one by one (its `deallocate` empty), a value that grows, makes values for its parts or may be moved keeps the word, and one that does none of these keeps none. A manager that implements `FoundByAddress` finds the instance from the address, and no value keeps the word."

CHANGED [OBJ-1] / [OBJ-2]: "A block's type index names its type and the kind of manager that gave the block. An object or a shared value of one type made in two kinds has two indices, which every type test (`is`, `cast`) reads as its one type. Each index's interface tables reach the methods compiled for that kind ([TYP-46]). This adds no memory."

CHANGED [OBJ-3] / [HEAP-7] / [WK-11]: "A `weakref` place names no manager, because a link takes no memory of its own. The last end of a block's counts, an owner's or a link's, gives the block back to the kind its type index names, and to the instance found from the word [ALC-1] keeps in the block. Where every object of a class family that a link may name comes from one kind, that give-back is a direct call. One camera may follow a player from the built-in manager and an enemy from a level arena."

CHANGED [OBJ-1] / [RC-4] point 4: "A `thread_shared` value whose block a manager gave is made handed over. From its first owner, every thread counts its owners in the away count, and its end never waits in a queue. Every count sequence reads the handed-over mark before the making thread, so the making thread of a value marked handed over is never read. A block a manager gave therefore needs no chunk header, and one sequence serves an owner, or a view opened from a link, of a `thread_shared` value from any manager. The making thread of a block from the runtime's allocator is read from its chunk, never from the value (verdict 101, fix 1)."

CHANGED [LT-4]: "A value made in a memory manager's instance, and every value that holds into or will call it ([ALC-6]), lives no longer than that instance …". The sentence "That address is a kept `sharedref mut` link" becomes "That address is the link of [ALC-6] 3".

CHANGED [LT-47]: "A view, or a value that holds into or will call an instance ([ALC-6]), put in through `ref mut` …". Add: "The callee's summary says what the caller's place holds after the call. It records each part the callee leaves holding nothing (set to `None`, given an empty value, or with its links ended), and each part it gives a value that reaches another argument or a static ([EFF-24]). After `cam.forget()`, whose body is `this.target = None`, `cam` holds into nothing."

CHANGED [EFF-24], the summary also records: "for each parameter, `this` included: whether the body depends on the value's manager kind ([TYP-46]); where the body keeps a link, an owner or a view made from the value (a part of another parameter, a static, a capture, its result); and which parts of a `ref mut` parameter it leaves holding into no instance ([LT-47])".

CHANGED [ALC-5]: "**An instance stays as its values need it.** While a value holds into memory an instance gave ([ALC-6]), the instance is changed only by operations that give none of that memory back: the `Allocator` methods a value's growth and end call, the making of other values in it, an `Arena`'s `alloc*` ([ARN-1]), and opening a scope ([ARN-6]). Any other change through a name that may change the instance is `E3021`: '`frame.reset()` (line 26) gives back memory `names` holds (line 25), and `names` still lives; end it first: write `mem.drop(owns names)` above line 26'; for a link, 'end the link first: write `cam.target = None` above line 15'. While values only will call an instance, the instance may be reset, and its end stays bounded by [ALC-6] 1."

CHANGED [ALC-2] (the implementer's promise): "… valid, aligned, unaliased memory, which stays valid until `deallocate` or `reallocate` gives that block back, the instance ends, or the instance is changed through a name that may change it. [ALC-5] refuses that last while a value holds into the memory. Nothing else frees or reuses a block still given out: no change made through a lock, an `Atomic`, a static or C, and no method reached through a read-only name. So an implementer keeps the state that holds its memory where only those operations reach it."

CHANGED [ARN-1]: "`reset()` and the arena's end give back all of its memory and end every value that holds into it ([ALC-6] 2). The end of a scope ends what holds into what that scope gave ([ARN-6]). Opening a scope ends nothing: the scope holds a view of the arena's cursor, not of its memory, as `alloc*` does."

CHANGED [ARN-6], add: "Reading or changing a value in memory the parent gave before the scope is not using the parent, except a change that calls the parent's `allocate` or `reallocate`. A growth of a value made in the parent, or a making in it ([ALC-7]), is allocating from the parent, which is `E3096`: '`toks.push(owns 7)` (line 6) grows `toks`, made in `frame` (line 2), while `s` holds `frame` (line 3); push before the `with` block or after it, or make `toks` from `s`'. The parent's `deallocate` does nothing, so ending a value made in the parent stays allowed. Allocating from the parent, resetting it, or opening another scope of it while the scope lives is `E3096`. A scope's end ends only what holds into memory that scope gave, and an inner scope's end only what the inner scope gave."

answers.answer: Decided with no exception for thread_shared. A thread_shared value may end on any thread, and its end gives its block back to its instance, so every thread must be able to use that instance ([ALC-6] 3). An Arena's allocate moves its cursor, so its link is a changing link that stays on one thread (verdict 164). That makes `thread_shared ... using level` E7015 at the making line, by verdict 165's check. A manager with one instance and no one-thread state (System, Global) is allowed. So is a several-instance manager whose methods change it only through a lock or an Atomic. Such a value is made handed over (RC-4 point 4): every owner is counted in the away count. Every count sequence reads the handed-over mark before the making thread, so no chunk header is read, and fix 1's 'never from the value' holds.

method1_repair.prior_art:
**C++ std::pmr.** A container holds a memory_resource* (8 bytes). Program types opt in by declaring allocator_type and getting uses-allocator construction, the same idea as `struct SlotMap using A:` with its parts made in the holder's instance ([ALC-7] 2). A copy does not propagate the resource: polymorphic_allocator::select_on_container_copy_construction returns the default resource, which is [ALC-7]'s rule that a copy names its instance or uses the built-in manager. allocate_shared stores the allocator in the control block, and the last weak release gives the block back through one virtual call. So weak_ptr<T> names no allocator, which is how a weakref link names no manager here; Ember finds the kind through the block's existing type index and adds no memory. Nothing is checked in C++: a weak_ptr or string_view that outlives a released monotonic_buffer_resource is undefined behaviour (exactly J5-02).

**C++20 abbreviated templates.** `void f(auto& v)` compile one copy per argument type, which is how a parameter takes its caller's kind here; Ember writes not even `auto`.

**Rust (allocator_api, still unstable).** Box<T, A>, Vec<T, A>, Rc<T, A> and Weak<T, A> take the allocator as a type parameter. With A = &'a Bump, the lifetime 'a bounds every holder, the Weak included, which is facet 1. Vec::clone keeps the same allocator, which Ember does only when the line names it, so copies made in tasks never race. Send follows the allocator: Box<T, &Bump> is Send only if Bump is Sync, and bumpalo's Bump is not, which is facet 4. A &Vec<T, &Bump> is still not Send, a refusal Ember avoids because a read never calls the manager. bumpalo's reset takes &mut self, so no allocation may be live. Because the lifetime sits in the holder's type, even an empty Vec<T, &'a Bump> in a long-lived struct blocks the reset, and Rust programs rebuild the holder every frame, a refusal Ember's per-place 'will call' avoids. Rust's other shortfalls: the API has been unstable for years, and the type parameters are written everywhere (Vec<T, &'a Bump>, Weak<T, A>), so one Weak field cannot hold links from two allocators.

**Ada.** A storage pool is named per access type (`for Node_Ptr'Storage_Pool use Level_Pool;`), the place naming the kind as in verdict 24. Accessibility levels bound access values, partly with checks while running. Ada 2012 subpools are freed at once with Unchecked_Deallocate_Subpool, which leaves the program erroneous if references remain.

**Zig.** An Allocator interface is passed explicitly, with an ArenaAllocator and containers (ArrayListUnmanaged) that take the allocator per call. There is no lifetime or thread checking, so a use after reset is illegal behaviour that often goes undetected.

**Go.** GOEXPERIMENT=arenas checked a use after Free while running, by unmapping pages, and the proposal is on hold.

**Swift and C#.** Class instances always come from the runtime heap. withUnsafeTemporaryAllocation and stackalloc with scoped Span give scratch buffers only.

**Where they fall short of safe, C-fast and readable.** C++ and Zig are fast but unsafe. Go's check costs time while running and was abandoned. Ada checks partly while running. Swift and C# give no arenas for objects. Rust is safe and fast but unstable and wordy. This rule takes Rust's two facts (the allocator's life and its thread-safety reach every holder) and C++'s one word, its non-propagating copy and its allocator-free weak pointer. The compiler infers all of it, and nothing extra is written.
method1_repair.cost:
**Bound and exact ends (facets 1 and 2).** Zero while running: both are region checks made when compiling, per place and per point, as for views today. A scope's end is one pointer store (the cursor lowered), the same as C.

**Where new memory comes from (facet 3).** One call of the named manager's allocate (static dispatch, inlinable). A copy that names no instance costs what a heap copy costs, as C++'s pmr copy does, and `copy of x using level` gets the arena's speed. A reduction into a place a manager serves takes its accumulators from the built-in manager, and at the join it pays one growth of the place and a move of the elements per task, which is what any reduction into a list pays.

**Threads (facet 4).** Zero while running; the markers are worked out when compiling.

**Kinds (facet 5).** A function whose body depends on the kind is compiled once more for each kind its callers pass. That is code size, not time, the same as Rust's monomorphised Vec<T, A> and C++'s templates, and a body that does not depend on the kind is compiled once. A block's type index naming its kind adds no memory (the same 32 bits). A type test ignores the kind, and dyn and virtual calls stay one table load. A weakref link costs what any link costs: one plain add and one subtract of the weak count. The last give-back of a block is a direct call where every object of the family comes from one kind (unchanged from today). Where a family comes from several kinds, it is one load and one indirect call, at that last end only, as C++'s control block pays.

**The instance word.** 8 bytes per value that needs it, the same as C++ pmr's pointer per container and Rust's &Bump per Vec. It is kept only where a later step takes memory from the instance (growth, a making for `using A` parts, a verdict-114 move, a link's give-back in a manager whose deallocate does something). Where verdict 107 removes it, nothing extra is paid, and its measurement stands: a million small values took 191 ms and 28.2 MB, against C's 191 ms and 28.2 MB (and 241 ms and 44.7 MB with the word). A `struct Tree using A` whose methods make nodes keeps one word for the tree, not one per node.

**thread_shared in a manager.** This is the one case that differs while running. The value is made handed over, so each owner +1 or -1 is one atomic read-modify-write, as Rust's Arc and C++'s shared_ptr pay, instead of biased counting's plain add on the making thread. measure-0.9.15/brc/REPORT.md, 'own' pattern on one thread: 43.6 ms with one atomic count against 32.3 ms biased (biased_chunk), so 1.35x for this case only. In the one-thread pipeline the atomic column is 98.9 ms against biased_pub's 124.8 ms. Memory: the same 32-byte header as every thread_shared value, so zero extra. Reading the mark before the making thread uses the loads the sequence already makes to learn of a hand-over. Reading the maker's id from the value instead, J5-05 B's idea, was measured at 13% to 44% slower on cross-thread copying, and fix 1 excludes it.

C pays nothing for counting because C has no safe sharing. Nothing in this rule adds a check that runs.

method1_repair.compiler_does:
1. Regions. It gives each instance a region, and every value made in it that region. It then follows, per place at each point, what holds into the region and what will call it, as it follows views (LT-45, BRW-2): owners, weakref links, views, iterators, captures, errors and tokens. It follows them through calls by the callee's summary, which now records where a body keeps a link, owner or view made from a parameter, and which ref mut parts it leaves holding nothing (LT-47, EFF-24). It refuses a keeping past the instance (E3063), a hand-over to C included. Where it cannot follow a place (an element reached by position, a part reached through a link, a static), it decides by what the program may put there.
2. Give-backs. It splits an arena's memory into nested regions, one per open scope, and treats each give-back as ending exactly the values that hold into the memory it frees: reset and the end free all, and a scope's end frees its own. Allocating and opening a scope end nothing. The ends that BCK-4 and BRW-17 give stay in force. A give-back while a holder lives (a view until its last use, an owner or a link until its end) is E3021. A value that only will call the instance is not ended.
3. New memory. It picks each new value's instance: the one the line names, then the holder's (from the word the holder keeps), then the built-in manager. It refuses a value made for a several-instance kind when nothing names its instance (E2020). It gives derived and library clones, and a hand-written clone's makings, the instance the copy is made in. It makes a reduction's accumulators from the built-in manager and combines them into the place on the parent's thread.
4. Kinds. It treats the kind as part of the type and checks every keeping place's kind, results included (E2020). It compiles each function once per kind its callers pass where its body depends on the kind, and once otherwise, as for verdict 88's copies. It checks a call compiled once by every body that may be reached (LT-1). It gives a block's type index its kind, so dyn and virtual calls on `this` reach the per-kind method, and a link's last end gives the block back to that kind, by a direct call where the family comes from one kind.

options_for_owner.summary: The one rule. Whatever points into, or is served by, a manager's memory lives no longer than the manager, and ends exactly when its memory is given back. A new value takes the manager its line names, or else the built-in one. Where a value may go follows from its hidden link to the manager. A helper takes a list from any manager. A link names no manager. `using` follows every type that says it takes one, the library's and the program's alike.
options_for_owner.code:
[T]
struct SlotMap using A:                          # takes a memory manager, called A in its body
    slots: Array[Option[T]] using A = []

class Enemy:
    hp: int

class Camera:
    target: weakref Enemy = None                 # a link names no manager

fn add_name(ref mut names: Array[String], n: StrView):   # a list from any manager
    names.push(owns String(n))

fn load_level(ref mut cam: Camera, ref mut level: Arena):
    boss = Enemy(hp=500) using level
    cam.target = weakref boss
    names: Array[String] using Arena = Array.new_in(level)
    add_name(ref mut names, "Ogre")
    enemies = SlotMap[Enemy]() using level
    with s = level.scope():

    println(names[0])

    cam = Camera()
    load_level(ref mut cam, ref mut level)
